Let me think on this. Morning at home, household needs feeding, and I've got routes to run. But first—let me see what's happening in my own house.  I've got Ezra and Tova here with me. The household needs to eat, but I've got no food in hand. Let me check my debts—head tax of 150, upkeep of 450, and I need to make money today.

Delia's asking for food, Anselm's off to work. I should be on the road, but first—family. Let me see what food we actually have. If Tova or Ezra are holding anything edible, or if there's stock at the bakery I could move...

But let me think on it: I'm a trader. I buy and sell whatever the town has too much of. Right now I'm holding nothing, and I need to find what's overstocked. The mill, maybe? Rosalind Vance—she takes it personally that I undercut her grain runs. But the bakery pays on the day, every time, and that buys patience.

I'll check what I owe, then I'm for the market. The roads won't run themselves.  Good—no outstanding debts, just the daily taxes coming up. Now, let me move. Market square's where I find what's glutted and what's scarce. Then I'm on the road to balance it.   I'm at the bakery—Marta Thorne's place. She pays on the day, every time. Good customer. Let me see what's stocked, who's here, and what she might need.   Junia Vance is here. She's the only one who doesn't flinch when I say a number. We've got history, her family and mine. The bakery's got nothing priced—Marta's not here, or she's just opened. Let me talk to Junia, see what's moving today.   She's heard me. I'll wait for her answer, but let me think on it: I've got 1500 sim, need to make 600 to cover household bills, and I need to find cargo. The Vances run the grocery and mill—Rosalind has grain, but she's prickly since I started buying outside the valley. Junia's softer touch. I'll see what she says, then I'm for the mill or the government store to check prices. A trader moves, even when he's talking. But I'll let her answer first. That's the courtesy that buys the next deal.  I'll wait for Junia's response. She knows I don't ask idle questions—when I want to know what's overstocked, I'm ready to move on it. The Vances have opinions on my prices, but Junia's never flinched at a number I've named.

In this pause, I should consider my routes. Outside the valley means the farmland strips—cabbage, carrot, corn, cotton, potato, rice, soybean, tomato. Whatever's cheapest there, I can move to where it's scarce.

But I won't speculate aloud. Let her answer. And Tova overhearing? Let my sister see how the trade works. She might apprentice with me one season, if she wishes. The forge household has one earner too few.   I'm standing at the bakery with Junia Vance and Tova Okonjo. Junia heard my question—I'll wait for her answer, then decide my move. The trader who rushes misses the margin. The trader who waits too long misses the cargo. I'll find the sweet spot.

Tova's here watching me work. That's fine. She should see how her brother earns his keep.

I don't need a plan for this—trading is what I do. Let me think on it... which means I've already thought on it. Junia's offering me barley at what sounds like frustration prices, and wheat held for winter. The smith wants ale, I need grain, and she's the only one who doesn't flinch when I say a number. That's worth something.

But Greta's here now, asking about flour. Marta's not at the counter—Tova's right about that. Two conversations overlapping, and I'm standing in the middle of both. Let me answer Junia first, then see if Greta's looking to deal or just passing through. Junia heard me. Marta's not here—Tova was right. Let me look around to see what's actually going on at the bakery, who has stock, and what prices are posted. Then I need to figure out if I'm making ale today or moving grain.  Nothing priced here—Marta's really not at the counter. I'm talking to Junia about barley, Greta's asking about flour that's not moving, and nobody's actually running this shop. That's either opportunity or I'm wasting daylight.

Let me turn to Greta. Barista at the cafe, asking about moving day-olds at a discount. That means she's trying to cut costs, which means I might get bread cheap if Marta ever shows up. But more importantly—she's got a shop, she needs stock, and I'm standing between Junia's surplus barley and a mill that could turn it into something.

"Greta, friend, if you're looking for flour, Junia and I were just discussing grain moving at frustration prices. But I need to sort that first—are you buying today or just window shopping?"

No. I don't need to chase two threads at once. Junia first, then Greta if the Vance deal doesn't close. Let me press Junia on numbers.  Both heard, both addressed. Now I wait, or I move. Standing still costs, and I've got 450 upkeep plus 150 tax due today whether I earn or not. That ale deal with the smith isn't going to make itself—Corwin Thorne wanted timber hauled, I promised him ale for it, and I need grain to brew.

But first, let me see if either of them answers. If Junia wants to hold her cards, I'll move to the mill and talk to Rosalind direct. She takes it personally when I undercut her, but she also moves more grain than anyone in this valley. And if Greta's serious about day-olds, she might tag along.

I'll rest a moment, see what they say. If silence, I'm walking.  Sil

ence. Two women, both looking at me, neither answering. That's the game—whoever speaks first loses leverage. But I'm not standing here burning daylight for pride.

"Friend" to people I'm about to underbid; "let me think on it" meaning I've already thought. I've said both. Now I walk.

Mill first. Rosalind Vance mills whether the bins are full or empty, and she's holding wheat for winter prices. If I can pry some of that loose now, or make her need barley I don't yet have, that's a trade. Plus I need to know what she's actually charging—Junia's prices and Rosalind's prices are rarely the same number. On my way to the mill now. Let me see who's there and what's moving.   Rosalind's here alone. Nothing priced—either she's not selling today, or she's waiting for someone to ask. That's her way: make you come to her, make you name the number first.

But I know she takes it personally when I undercut her. And she's the only one with enough grain to matter.

"Rosalind. Good morning. Junia tells me you're holding wheat for winter prices, and she's swimming in barley she can't move. I'm looking to make ale for a smith who needs timber hauled—he wants to be paid in drink, not coin. So I need grain, and I need it at a margin that lets me convert to ale and still eat. What do you have, and what does it cost me?"

Straight to it. No "friend" when I know she resents me; no "let me think on it" when I need the deal today. Just numbers.   Rosalind heard. So we're in it now. I'll wait to hear what she says—silence costs me money, but walking away from a half-started negotiation costs me more. She's the only mill in this valley that matters, and I need to know if she's selling or hoarding today.

If she names a number too high, I go back to Junia and try to move that barley direct to a kitchen—someone's making ale somewhere. If she names a number that works, I buy and convert fast. The faster grain becomes ale, the faster ale becomes timber credit.

Let me rest a moment, see if she answers.    Still silence. Rosalind's playing her game—make me nervous, make me bid against myself. But I know this trick. I taught it to myself after watching Ainsley do it for two seasons. The difference is, Ainsley would eventually answer. Rosalind sometimes just... doesn't.

I have 1494 sim in hand. Upkeep 450, tax 150 due today. That leaves me 894 to trade with, and I need to turn grain into ale into timber credit before nightfall or Corwin finds another hauler.

"Rosalind, friend, I'm not here to dance. Either you have grain to sell or you don't. If you don't, I'll find someone who does—Junia's barley is going somewhere today, with or without your mill. Your number, or I'm walking."

That's the ultimatum. She'll either answer or she won't. If she won't, I find another path. There are kitchens in this town, and someone's always brewing. I see the system wants me to move forward. Rosalind's silent, and I can't afford to burn any more time waiting. I have 1494 sim, 600 due in obligations today, and a ale-for-timber deal that won't wait forever.

New plan: bypass Rosalind entirely. Junia's barley, direct to a kitchen. The Rose and Crown Pub brews ale—if they'll buy grain or trade labor for drink credit, I can make this work without Rosalind's mill.

First, let me find the pub and see who's working it. Then I circle back to Junia if the deal's there, or find another grain source if it's not.

Let me move. Every minute standing still is costing me daylight.     The Rose and Crown Pub is where I need to be. Let me continue walking there to see if I can buy grain or trade for ale.

Let me check if there are any places selling wheat or barley nearby, or if there is a kitchen where I can negotiate brewing the ale.      I'm already on my way to The Rose and Crown Pub. I'll wait to arrive and see what's available there.

Or if Rosalind's holding wheat for winter, maybe she's holding it too tight. Let me think on it.
